assumptions.summary: Every replacement is a double-curvature concrete arch dam with reservoir and hydropower station.
Dam construction cost increases with dam size.
On-way resistance is proportional to current velocity with a constant coefficient.
Evaporation is constant within the adopted model regions.
Pressure variation in x is neglected and rain enters with zero horizontal velocity.
Headstream v and h are constant; initial h is uniform and v follows a free-fall expression.
The HM uses L(x)=1 km throughout the river.
Lake, pocket-lowland, and valley suitability are encoded as zero or one.
Velocity variation is neglected within the DM period T.
Gate discharge follows a three-halves head law and three discrete openings.
One beta and one alpha represent collision loss and precipitation-runoff conversion.
One three-month flood and one three-month drought stand in for extreme operating states.

contributions.summary: An eight-stage roadmap connects stakeholder comparison, physics, siting, recurrence, construction, operation, and testing.
Each official option receives an explicit need-cost-work-benefit profile before detailed modeling.
Local mass and energy balances expose the physical inputs and output fields required downstream.
Model outputs and independent terrain, hydrology, landform, and width evidence form one candidate matrix.
A dam-indexed Difference Model creates a tractable state interface for repeated design and policy evaluation.
Tributaries, loss, and rainfall-runoff forcing are restored before structural and operational decisions.
A visible initialize-simulate-check-upgrade loop communicates a discrete safety-cost heuristic.
Parallel flood and drought contracts turn a fixed design into scenario-specific manager actions.
A repeated perturbation-table-interpretation structure tests three output families.
Each declared data or scope gap is matched to a targeted future evidence need.

independent_extensions.summary: Replace raw-unit GRA with direction-correct, dimensionless value functions and a sensitivity-tested weighting method.
Derive a unit-consistent Saint-Venant or shallow-water baseline and verify the reduced recurrence against it.
Use GIS-based candidate generation and a disclosed constrained subset optimizer for number and placement.

models.summary: Repair costs are taken from the World Bank rehabilitation project, rebuilding costs from historic Stage 1 component expenditure, and distributed replacement from discrete dam-type counts plus institutional support.
A short river control volume balances inflow, rainfall, evaporation, outflow, and storage, then substitutes rectangular-channel geometry and takes a differential form.
The paper balances gravity and resistance work against kinetic-energy changes, closes resistance as proportional to velocity, simplifies rainfall and evaporation kinematics, and obtains a second PDE.

models.section: HM Boundary, Initial Conditions, and Numerical Calculation
models.summary: Headstream velocity and depth are constant, initial depth is uniform, initial velocity follows a free-fall profile, altitude is interpolated from Google Earth, rainfall is fitted, and Mathematica produces velocity and depth curves.

models.section: Selection System - Evaluation Indexes and Candidate Sites
models.summary: The paper defines eight criteria with stated good directions, encodes three topographic features as binary indicators, and selects 26 candidate sites from relief, rainfall, modeled depth, and spacing considerations.
The seven-step method chooses an ideal reference, computes absolute differences and extrema, forms grey coefficients and relation degrees, normalizes criterion weights, and scores each candidate.

models.section: Difference Model - River Reach Without a Dam
models.summary: For reach i and time period j, the model writes continuity and energy balances, estimates mean velocity and kinetic-energy change from upstream/downstream fluxes, and obtains a coupled discrete reach equation.
The dam region uses a storage balance, a three-halves hydraulic discharge relation, and a gate coefficient proportional to opening and hole width.
Equation 32 solves for reach outflow, computes gated discharge, and advances both river and reservoir depths so the state at period j becomes the input at period j+1.
The paper maps tributaries to reaches, multiplies the elevation-energy contribution by beta, and makes the headstream and five tributary flows linear functions of net rainfall through alpha.
The paper starts every site at the smallest type, simulates the corrected DM, upgrades a dam after a warning violation, repeats until stable, and then checks a system capacity inequality.

The paper treats smaller seasonal fluctuation as better Lake protection, runs the corrected DM for rainy and dry periods, and qualitatively claims the proposed system reduces fluctuation while offering three gate choices.

The paper fixes a flood location, duration, and rainfall intensity, simulates every gear combination with corrected DM, rejects warning violations, minimizes the variance of depth deviations, and reports one A-vector.

The drought section mirrors the flood protocol: it fixes forcing, computes an unregulated baseline, enumerates gate combinations, evaluates a runoff-increase objective, and reports maximum opening at every dam.

The paper perturbs four inputs over a symmetric seven-point percentage grid, recomputes three output families, records maximum relative change in Tables 5-7, and classifies two outputs as insensitive and runoff as sensitive.

results_trace.summary: Reported totals are US$294.2m for repair, US$1,109.7m for rebuild, and US$929.6m for replacement including support.
Velocity and river-depth curves are reported as approaching stable spatial states.
Twenty-six candidate dam sites are retained for multicriteria evaluation.
Eleven sites A-K are selected at distances 120, 420, 738, 806, 825, 885, 1208, 1408, 1683, 1715, and 1885 km.
Table 3 reports types III, III, III, III, III, III, III, IV, I, IV, and III for A-K.
The proposed system is stated to reduce seasonal Lake fluctuation and provide three management gears.
The reported A vector is 4, 8, 16, 16, 16, 16, 16.5, 5.5, 16.5, 8, and 8.
The selected flood strategy is presented as keeping reservoir states nearer normal and warning limits.
Every dam is assigned its maximum A_i in the reported drought strategy.
H and h are called insensitive while Q is called sensitive, especially to initial reservoir depth.
The authors propose extending the corrected multi-dam system to other rivers after obtaining better data and broader criteria.

weaknesses.summary: Equation 32's printed Q' recurrence is not the quadratic solution of Equation 28: coefficients that should contain q_ij-delta_ij are replaced by g, and Equation 33 inherits the substitution.
The collision-loss factor beta multiplies the gravitational elevation term; beta=0.001 therefore suppresses 99.9% of gravity rather than adding a derived head-loss mechanism.
The nominal capacity inequality is infeasible with the printed catalog: eleven type-I dams provide only 66 km^3, and the reported mix about 6.326 km^3, versus Lake Kariba's 180 km^3.
The prose fixes dam 11 as type I and dam 7 as type II, but Table 3 reports both as type III, places the only type I at dam 9, and reports no type II.
Table 1 gives 8 type-III plus 2 type-IV construction cost as US$7.6m, not US$860m; neither that vector nor Table 3 reconciles to the claimed US$929.6m option total.
Table 2 calls S reservoir area while the prose treats types as capacity classes; S_i H_mi ignores geometry and live-versus-dead storage, and no explicit cost objective closes the tradeoff.
Figure 16 upgrades the dam with minimum H-H_m after a violation, which can target an already-safe dam rather than the largest exceedance; no optimizer or tie rule is supplied.

The resistance derivation is dimensionally inconsistent: if F_r=kv is resistance per volume, work requires travel distance v Delta t, while Equation 13 and the resulting Equation 16 do not preserve compatible units.

The discrete energy model silently changes the resistance parameter by introducing rho*k while retaining the continuous-model k definition, so the HM and DM do not share one unit-consistent coefficient.
The printed Delta(v^2) expansion misses a factor of two, and Equation 16 omits the free-surface gradient after neglecting pressure variation; it is not a complete open-channel momentum law.

Q shifts from a mass-like quantity containing rho in Equations 1-7 to volumetric discharge in the DM, while q shifts among rainfall amount, depth rate, and tributary flow; symbol ownership is unstable.
With T=60 s, 90,000 iterations equal 5.4 million seconds or 62.5 days, not the claimed three months used for seasonal and emergency conclusions.
The HM fixes river width at 1 km while the site matrix uses widths from about 0.089 to 2.133 km, so upstream hydrodynamics and downstream site scoring use incompatible channel geometry.
Rainfall plots are monthly or annual millimeters while q in the PDE requires m/s; no conversion or fitted function is published, so the forcing is not dimensionally traceable or reproducible.
v0, h0, k, alpha, beta, tributary flows, and initial depths are estimates without calibration or provenance; the parameter ledger also prints g as m/s rather than m/s^2.

The Mathematica solver, domain, mesh, time step, boundary compatibility, fit coefficients, residuals, mass balance, and convergence checks are absent, so the stable-state claim in Figures 7-8 is not demonstrated.
Equation 23 combines slope, acceleration, rainfall, depth, binary flags, and width in raw incompatible units, making the GRA score dependent on arbitrary measurement scales.
The largest-value ideal is inconsistent with the negative terrain-gap values in Table 11 and can prefer flat or uphill sites; the width direction reversal is stated but not transparently implemented.
Criterion weights are averages of candidate similarity to the ideal rather than preference or importance evidence; the reported analysis omits the weights and lambda sensitivity.

The reduction from 26 scores to eleven sites uses undocumented cost-and-distance clustering; no threshold, objective, cluster count, assignments, or cost function is given, while a later strength claim names absent k-means.
Table 4 contains controls outside the declared type-specific gear sets: A7=16.5 is impossible for type III and A10=8 is impossible for type IV.
The Lake-protection section references a missing figure and supplies no fluctuation value, current-dam baseline, common seasonal forcing, or statistical comparison for its improvement claim.

Minimizing variance of H_i-H_i0 does not directly minimize downstream flood discharge or inundation; no floodplain, routing, exposed-population, or economic-protection metric connects the objective to stated stakes.
The drought text assigns delta_i, defined as evaporation, the value 'rainfall 1100 mm/year' and calls it heavy rain, conflating variable, unit, and scenario meaning.

The drought flowchart follows the objective branch when any dam is below stable level, reversing a storage-feasibility check; all-maximum release has no terminal-storage or sustained-service constraint.
Figure 22's caption says reservoir depth, while the axis and prose identify runoff Q in m^3/s, so the visual's measured state is mislabeled.
The sensitivity prose perturbs Q1 while Tables 5-7 use undefined Q00; Q, Q', q', H0j, and H0i indexing leaves the tested input ambiguous.
The sensitivity values contain unexplained discontinuities, including nearly constant nonzero H response to Q00 around a zero baseline response and a Q response returning to zero only at +5% h_i0.

The paper calls H and h insensitive despite up to 11.4852% H and 28.3529% Q response; one-at-a-time output changes do not test selected sites, types, gears, joint uncertainty, or recommendation reversals.

One assumed flood and one assumed drought do not validate 'most extreme conditions'; the requested location and last occurrence time of a specific event and any historical or out-of-sample validation are absent.
